aspects.says: Moving the compound action into the class that owns the lock, as one synchronized method, leaves no lock for a caller to forget.
basis: section:The Compound Action Belongs in the Class That Owns the Lock

aspects.says: Synchronized single methods on a class don't make a caller's check followed by an act atomic.
basis: section:A Lock Written at Each Call Site Is Missing at the Site That Forgets It

aspects.says: An action or a read across two thread-safe objects is not atomic; the lock for a rule over both belongs to one object that owns both.
basis: section:An Action Across Two Wallets Needs One Owner for Both Balances

aspects.says: When each caller locks around a compound action on a shared object, one caller that forgets the lock can overwrite the others' updates, locked callers included.
basis: section:A Lock Written at Each Call Site Is Missing at the Site That Forgets It

aspects.says: A shared withLock helper removes repeated text but leaves each caller composing the action, so a caller that skips it still compiles and races.
basis: section:The Compound Action Belongs in the Class That Owns the Lock

aspects.says: Removing the setter that callers composed the action from makes javac report every such call site, locked or not.
basis: section:The Compound Action Belongs in the Class That Owns the Lock
aspects.reason: a compile error is what shows it; a graded test cannot run a compile that is meant to fail, so the page shows the javac run

aspects.says: Every method of the class that touches the guarded state takes the same lock; a second lock inside the class lets updates under the other one be lost.
basis: section:The Compound Action Belongs in the Class That Owns the Lock

aspects.says: Clean stress runs are a sample; the argument that the class is safe is that its state is touched only under one lock in one class.
basis: section:The Compound Action Belongs in the Class That Owns the Lock
